result.summary: Adds a request completion deadline to Bitcoin Core's HTTP server to disconnect clients that take too long to send a complete request. The deadline is armed when the first byte of a request is received, expires after -rpcservertimeout, and is not extended by subsequent reads. It is cleared once request parsing completes, deferred while worker threads process a request, and restarted while response bytes are actively going out.
result.problem: The existing -rpcservertimeout only tracks inactivity between reads. A client trickling bytes indefinitely without completing a request continually resets the idle timer, permanently occupying an HTTP connection slot without ever hitting RPC authentication. Because connection slots are capped by default at 16 (or -rpcmaxconnections), such clients can exhaust all available slots and prevent any legitimate RPC requests from being accepted.
evidence: The author provides a concrete reproduction: starting a node with -rpcmaxconnections=2, opening two sockets, and trickling 'GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n' one byte every ten seconds causes bitcoin-cli getblockcount to hang indefinitely.

Description notes: 'Connection slots are capped by default 16 or by -rpcmaxconnections. Once those slots are taken, the server stops accepting new connections. Because no request ever completes the authentication functions are never hit.'
result.changed_since_previous: No substantial changes to the implementation mechanism; the core logic and test coverage remain as previously described.
result.card: Adds a request completion deadline to the HTTP server to disconnect clients that fail to finish sending an HTTP request within the -rpcservertimeout interval. Currently, the timeout only measures inactivity between reads and resets on every received byte, allowing a slowloris-style trickle of bytes to hold an HTTP connection slot indefinitely without triggering authentication checks. Because connection slots are capped at 16 by default, exhausted slots prevent legitimate RPC callers from connecting. The author notes that because the RPC interface binds to localhost by default, this functions as a local robustness improvement rather than a remote denial-of-service fix.

risk.why: Flaws in HTTP connection lifetime or deadline resetting could prematurely disconnect legitimate RPC/REST clients or cause denial of service on local node management.
